title: Reading earned value: variances & indices
blurb: Interpret cost and schedule variances, CPI and SPI, and the estimate at completion, and decide what action each one calls for.
question: A logistics firm's warehouse system project reports a schedule performance index of 0.9 and a cost performance index of 1.1 at month six. The sponsor wants to know whether to be pleased or worried, and what the project manager will do next. How should these figures be interpreted?

teach.h: Two variances, two indices, one forecast
teach.body: Earned value turns PV, EV and AC into signals. Variances are differences in money: cost variance CV = EV − AC, schedule variance SV = EV − PV. Indices are ratios: CPI = EV ÷ AC, SPI = EV ÷ PV. Notice that EV comes first every time, so a NEGATIVE variance or an index BELOW 1 is bad news, while positive or above 1 is better than plan. The exam asks you to interpret these, never to calculate them.

Compares

Good news
teach.caption: Zero variance or an index of exactly 1 means exactly on plan.

cells.label: Ahead, under budget
cells.sub: Check it's real, not luck or missed invoices

cells.label: Ahead, over budget
cells.sub: Buying speed? Is it worth it?

cells.label: Behind, under budget
cells.sub: Often under-resourced: little spent, little done

teach.caption: Month 6 (illustrative): PV £150k, EV £135k, AC £123k. EV below PV: behind schedule (SV negative, SPI about 0.9). EV above AC: the work done cost less than budgeted (CV positive, CPI about 1.1). The cause? Two developers were moved off the project. Less spent, but less done: the 'saving' is really a delay, and the missing work still has to be paid for.

teach.body: The estimate at completion (EAC) forecasts the total cost of the project given performance so far. The estimate to complete (ETC) is the cost of the remaining work. Compare EAC with the budget at completion (BAC): if CPI stays below 1, EAC rises above BAC and the project will overrun unless something changes. Illustration only: a £300k project running at a CPI of 0.9 is heading for roughly £333k. Forecasts are refined every period as trends become clearer.

teach.h: Watch the trend, not one snapshot
teach.caption: A CPI sliding month after month is an early warning: each month the EAC climbs further above the BAC. Acting in month 3 is far cheaper than in month 9.

items: Investigate the cause: rates, productivity, estimating errors, scope creep, invoice timing.
For schedule slippage, check the critical path: SV is in money, so a slip in work with float may not move the end date.
Take corrective action within tolerance: re-plan, re-sequence, rebalance resources, value-engineer, or draw contingency for risks that occurred.
Update the EAC and report the trend honestly.
If the forecast breaches tolerance, escalate to the sponsor with options (an exception or change request).

teach.text: Three exam traps. 1: Actual cost below planned value does NOT mean under budget: cost performance needs EV. 2: SV is measured in money, not days, and SPI above 1 doesn't prove the critical path is on time. 3: A positive CV isn't automatically good news: check that quality hasn't been cut and invoices aren't just late.

rows.label: Main question
values: Will we finish on budget and time?
How much scope will the budget buy?

rows.label: Key signals
values: CV, SV, CPI, SPI and EAC

teach.caption: Iterative time and cost are fixed per time box, so poor performance usually shows as less scope delivered rather than a cost overrun.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the measure and what it compares (for example CPI compares earned value with actual cost).
Interpret its direction: negative or below 1 is worse than plan; positive or above 1 is better.
Read cost and schedule together and suggest a likely cause in the scenario.
State the action: investigate, correct within tolerance, update the EAC, escalate if tolerance is breached.
CV = EV − AC: negative means over budget. SV = EV − PV: negative means behind schedule.
CPI and SPI: below 1 is worse than plan, above 1 better, exactly 1 on plan.
EAC forecasts total cost; EAC above BAC means a forecast overrun.
Read indices together and as trends; always look for the cause.
Act within tolerance, escalate beyond it.

summary: You can now interpret cost and schedule variances, CPI and SPI, alone and in combination, and explain what an estimate at completion above or below budget means. You can also say what action a project manager should take in response, and how this differs in iterative delivery.

A.q: A project's cost performance index (CPI) is 0.85. What does this indicate?
options: The work done has cost more than budgeted
The project is 15% ahead of its schedule
The work done has cost less than budgeted
The project has used 85% of its budget
A.why: CPI below 1 means less than £1 of budgeted work is being earned for each £1 spent: the work done is costing more than planned.

whyNot.1: CPI measures cost efficiency, not schedule; schedule is shown by SPI.
whyNot.2: That would be a CPI above 1.
whyNot.3: CPI is a ratio of earned value to actual cost, not the proportion of budget spent.

A.q: A monthly report shows a negative schedule variance. What does this tell the project manager?
options: Less money has been spent than planned
The work done has cost more than budget
The final cost will exceed the budget
Less work has been done than planned
A.why: SV = EV − PV. Negative means the value of work done is less than the value of work planned by now: the project is behind schedule.

whyNot.0: Comparing spend with plan isn't SV; SV compares work done with work planned.
whyNot.1: Work costing more than budgeted is a negative cost variance.
whyNot.2: A forecast overrun is shown by EAC above BAC, not by SV alone.

A.q: Earned value equals planned value exactly, but actual cost is higher than both. How is the project performing?
options: Behind schedule and over budget
On schedule but over budget
Ahead of schedule, on budget
On schedule and under budget
A.why: EV = PV means the planned work has been done (on schedule). AC above EV means that work cost more than budgeted (over budget).

whyNot.0: EV equals PV, so the work is not behind.
whyNot.2: Ahead would need EV above PV, and AC above EV means over budget, not on budget.
whyNot.3: AC above EV means overspending, not under budget.

B.q: A project reports an SPI of 1.1 and a CPI of 0.9. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Behind schedule and under budget
Ahead of schedule but over budget
Behind schedule and over budget
Ahead of schedule and under budget
B.why: SPI above 1 means more work done than planned (ahead); CPI below 1 means that work cost more than budgeted (over budget). The team may be buying speed, for example with overtime.

whyNot.0: SPI above 1 is ahead, and CPI below 1 is over budget: this reverses both.
whyNot.2: SPI above 1 means ahead, not behind.
whyNot.3: CPI below 1 means over budget, not under.

B.q: The latest estimate at completion (EAC) is now higher than the budget at completion (BAC). What does this suggest?
options: The project has already exceeded its budget
Contingency should be returned to the sponsor
The project will overrun unless things change
The schedule must have slipped behind plan
B.why: EAC is a forecast of total cost based on performance so far. Above BAC means a forecast overrun if current trends continue, so action is needed now.

whyNot.0: EAC is a forecast; the overrun hasn't necessarily happened yet.
whyNot.1: A forecast overrun is the opposite of a reason to release contingency.
whyNot.3: EAC is a cost forecast and doesn't by itself show schedule performance.

B.q: A project shows a healthy positive cost variance, but the client has started rejecting deliverables for poor finish. What should the project manager conclude?
options: The saving may come from cutting corners
The cost variance proves quality is fine
The budget was set far too high at the start
The schedule variance must also be positive
B.why: A positive CV isn't automatically good. Combined with rejected work, it may mean the saving comes from cutting quality, and rework will erode it. EVM doesn't measure quality.

whyNot.1: EVM says nothing about quality, so a positive CV can't prove it.
whyNot.2: An over-generous budget is possible, but the rejections point to a quality cause that must be checked first.
whyNot.3: Cost and schedule variances are independent; one doesn't imply the other.

C.q: A project reports SPI 0.8 and CPI 1.05. The PM learns that two team members were moved to other work last month. What is the MOST likely explanation?
options: Efficient work is saving money on every task
Fewer people means little spent but little done
The baseline budget was approved at the wrong level
Contingency was drawn down to cover the losses
C.why: With fewer people, less money is spent and less work is done. The project looks under budget only because the delayed work hasn't been paid for yet; it is really slipping.

whyNot.0: Efficiency would not explain falling well behind schedule at the same time.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests a baseline error; the scenario points to a resourcing cause.
whyNot.3: Drawing contingency increases spend; it wouldn't explain low spend and slow progress.

C.q: A project's schedule variance is negative, but all the delayed activities have plenty of float. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: The end date has certainly slipped
The project must be over budget too
The end date may not be affected yet
The variance should simply be ignored
C.why: SV is measured in money and doesn't show whether the critical path is affected. If the delayed work has float, the end date may hold, but the PM should keep watching so the float isn't used up.

whyNot.0: Delays in activities with float don't necessarily move the end date.
whyNot.1: Schedule and cost performance are separate; SV says nothing about cost.
whyNot.3: Float can be consumed; the variance should be monitored, not ignored.

C.q: CPI has fallen for three months and the EAC now exceeds the cost tolerance delegated to the project manager. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Keep going and hope the trend recovers
Spend management reserve without asking
Stop reporting the CPI until it improves
Escalate to the sponsor with options
C.why: A forecast beyond tolerance is outside the PM's authority, so it must be escalated to the sponsor (for example by exception report) with causes, options and recommendations.

whyNot.0: A sustained trend rarely corrects itself, and the tolerance breach requires escalation.
whyNot.1: Management reserve is held by the sponsor or board; the PM can't spend it unilaterally.
whyNot.2: Hiding performance data breaks governance and removes the early warning.

reteach.title: A road trip on a fuel budget
reteach.question: You plan to drive 400 miles in eight hours on £60 of fuel. Four hours in, how do you know whether you're behind, and whether fuel will run out?

blocks.h: Miles covered is your earned value
blocks.body: By hour four you planned 200 miles (planned value). You've actually covered 160 miles (earned value): behind schedule, like an SPI below 1. You've used £30 of fuel, but 160 miles should only have used £24 (actual cost above earned value): poor fuel efficiency, like a CPI below 1. If nothing changes, the whole trip will cost more than £60: that is your estimate at completion beating your budget. Time to ease off the accelerator, or ring ahead.

blocks.text: Fuel used versus fuel planned (AC versus PV) tells you nothing on its own: you need the miles actually covered (EV).

explain.body: Both compare earned value with actual cost. CV gives the gap in money (negative means over budget); CPI gives efficiency (below 1 means each £1 spent earns less than £1 of planned work).

explain.caption: AC climbing above EV: CV negative, CPI below 1. EV also below PV: behind schedule.

test.q: Which measure shows how efficiently money is being turned into completed work?
options: Schedule performance index
Budget at completion
Planned value
Cost performance index
test.why: CPI compares earned value with actual cost, showing how much budgeted work each £1 of spend is achieving.

whyNot.0: SPI measures progress against the schedule, not cost efficiency.
whyNot.1: BAC is the total budget, not a performance measure.
whyNot.2: PV is the planned work to date, not a measure of efficiency.

explain.body: Both compare earned value with planned value. SV is in money (negative means behind); SPI below 1 means work is progressing slower than planned. Neither tells you directly whether the critical path is affected.

test.q: A project's SPI is exactly 1.0. What does this mean?
options: The work done matches the plan
The project is exactly on budget
The project has finished on time
No money has been spent so far
test.why: SPI = 1 means earned value equals planned value: the work done to date is exactly what was scheduled.

whyNot.1: SPI says nothing about cost; that's CPI.
whyNot.2: SPI of 1 can occur at any point, not just at the end.
whyNot.3: SPI compares EV with PV; it isn't about spend.

explain.body: The estimate at completion forecasts the final cost from performance so far; the estimate to complete is what the remaining work will cost. EAC above BAC signals a forecast overrun; EAC below BAC a forecast underrun.

test.q: The EAC has fallen below the BAC. What does this suggest, if current performance continues?
options: The schedule is ahead
A forecast overrun
A forecast underrun
Contingency is spent
test.why: EAC below BAC means the project is forecast to finish for less than its budget, assuming current trends hold.

whyNot.0: EAC is a cost forecast; it doesn't show schedule.
whyNot.1: An overrun would be EAC above BAC.
whyNot.3: EAC below BAC doesn't indicate contingency has been used.

explain.body: Numbers only matter if they prompt action. Within tolerance, the PM investigates causes, corrects course and updates the forecast. Beyond tolerance, the PM escalates to the sponsor with options. Favourable variances are checked too, in case they hide problems.

test.q: A small negative cost variance is well within the PM's agreed tolerance. What should the PM do?
options: Escalate it at once to the board
Raise a formal change request
Investigate, correct and report
Do nothing until it gets worse
test.why: Within tolerance, the PM has authority to investigate the cause, take corrective action and report it in routine progress reports.

whyNot.0: Escalation is for forecasts beyond tolerance; this is within it.
whyNot.1: Change requests are for changes to the baseline, not routine corrective action.
whyNot.3: Small variances can grow; early action is the purpose of EVM.
